input: The Prandtl number is an extremely useful dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of heat transfer, and it can be understood as a comparison between two different ways in which a fluid spreads things out. On the one hand, momentum diffusivity describes how rapidly differences in velocity are smoothed out across a moving fluid, while on the other hand, thermal diffusivity describes how rapidly differences in temperature are smoothed out across the same fluid. The Prandtl number is, in essence, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, and it therefore captures, in a single number, which of these two smoothing processes is the faster one for a given fluid. When the Prandtl number takes a value near 1, the two diffusivities are broadly comparable in size, which means that momentum and heat spread through the fluid at similar rates. When, by contrast, the Prandtl number is large, momentum diffusivity is much greater than thermal diffusivity, so velocity differences are ironed out over a much wider region than temperature differences, which remain confined to a comparatively thin layer. Where the Prandtl number falls below 1, the position is reversed: thermal diffusivity is then the greater of the two, and temperature differences are spread over a wider region than velocity differences.
target:
The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity states how fast velocity differences even out across a fluid; thermal diffusivity states how fast temperature differences even out. The Prandtl number compares the two rates for one fluid, and its size states which process spreads farther.

A value near 1 means the two diffusivities are comparable. Momentum and heat then spread at similar rates, and the velocity and temperature fields adjust over similar distances from a surface. A large value means momentum diffuses much faster than heat. Velocity differences are smoothed across a thick layer, while temperature differences persist in a thinner layer near the surface, so the temperature field is the more confined of the two. A value below 1 reverses the comparison: heat diffuses faster than momentum, and the temperature field spreads beyond the velocity field.

The Prandtl number is a property comparison, not a flow measurement. It ranks two diffusivities of the fluid itself, and it states nothing about any particular flow until it is combined with the quantities that describe that flow.

The two diffusivities belong to the fluid, not to the flow. Geometry, speed and size enter a heat-transfer calculation through other quantities; the Prandtl number contributes only the comparison between the two rates at which the fluid itself smooths out differences. Read that way, the number is a statement about the fluid's internal behaviour, made before any apparatus is specified.
